desc:
Place every node of a binary tree at a coordinate (row, column): the root is at (0, 0); the left child of a node at (row, col) is at (row + 1, col - 1) and its right child is at (row + 1, col + 1).

Report the values column by column, from the smallest column number to the largest. Inside a column list the nodes by increasing row; if several nodes of the same column are in the same row, list them by increasing value (equal values simply appear next to each other). The empty tree gives [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 5, 7] the nodes 5 and 6 share the position row 2, column 0 and are ordered by value, so the answer is [[4], [2], [1, 5, 6], [3], [7]]. (With “left to right” tie-breaking, the middle column would be [1, 6, 5].)
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Give each node a triple of (column, row, value) and think about which ordering of the triples gives exactly the requested output.
Sorting the triples lexicographically by column, then row, then value already puts everything in the right order. A plain BFS is no longer enough because of the value tie-break.
Traverse the tree computing row and column for each node, collect the triples, sort them, and cut the sorted list into groups of equal column.
editorial: The required order is exactly the lexicographic order on (column, row, value). So compute the row and the column of every node (parents are always listed before children in the level-order array, which makes this one pass), put the triples into a list, sort it, and then split the sorted list into groups that share a column value.

Sorting costs O(n log n). Compared with the version where ties are resolved from left to right, the difference is that two nodes can only compete when they have the same row and the same column, and then the smaller value must go first, so the left-to-right order of a plain level-order walk cannot be relied on. An alternative that avoids the global sort is to keep a bucket per column and sort each bucket, but the single sort is simplest.
